label: final sweep — conic algebra, function composition, polar roots, similarity proportion

widget.prompt: x² − 6x becomes a perfect square once the right constant is added. Build the completed square and read what landed at k.
widget.successFeedback: The vertex settles at (3, 0) — nothing left over, which is exactly what 'perfect square' means. That vertex says x² − 6x + 9 = (x − 3)², so the constant added was 9: half of −6, squared.
widget.shapeFeedback: Leave a at 1; there is no coefficient on x² here.
widget.vertexFeedback: Not a perfect square yet — half of −6 is −3, so the vertex belongs at x = 3.

widget.prompt: a² = 4 asks: what number, squared, gives 4? Slide the base until base² reads 4.
widget.successFeedback: Base 2, so 2² = 4 confirms a = 2 — the same relationship as a² = 4, read forward instead of solved backward. Dividing 9x² − 4y² = 36 by 36 was the whole job; finding a is just this one square root.

widget.prompt: Every cube root of 8 shares the same modulus. Slide the base until base^(1/3) reads 2.
widget.successFeedback: 8^(1/3) = 2 — and that is the modulus every one of the three cube roots shares, however different their angles are. Roots of a complex number fan out around a circle of exactly this radius; only the angle changes between them.

widget.prompt: f(g(3)) works from the inside out. Trace g(x) = x² to x = 3 and read the height — that height becomes f's input next.
widget.successFeedback: g(3) = 9. Now feed that INTO f: f(9) = 2(9) − 1 = 17. Composition order matters because the output of the inner function becomes the input of the outer one — g first, then f on whatever g handed back.

widget.prompt: Three parallel lines cut one transversal into 6 and 9, and the other into 8 and x. Find the constant ratio from the first pair, then apply it.

numericErrors.feedback: 6.75 adds the gap (3) to 9 rather than scaling. The two transversals are proportional, not offset by a constant difference.
10.5 averages 9 and 12. The relationship is a RATIO — the same constant that turned 6 into 8 turns 9 into x.

widget.successFeedback: 8/6 = 4/3 is the constant ratio, and 9 × 4/3 = 12. Parallel lines cut every transversal they cross in the SAME proportion — that is the one fact both segments obey, on both lines, at once.
widget.explorationFeedback: Check the first pair (6, 8) before applying the ratio to the second.

refusals.why: DISCOVERED BY THE SCHEMA GATE. (x-2)²=8(y+1) rearranges to y=(1/8)(x-2)²-1, and quadraticExplore's targetA/aStart are BOTH .int() -- a constraint that happened to never bind in prior conversions because every earlier lesson's leading coefficient was already a whole number. 1/8 is fixed by the given equation (4p=8), not something reframing can change without altering the actual parabola. Refused -- the same class of gap as vectorExplore's integer coordinates (S203T) and expLogExplore's [0.2,10] grid (S203S): a schema constraint that widget-contract.ts's 'number' label does not distinguish from an unconstrained float.

refusals.title: Restricting the Domain
refusals.why: DISCOVERED BY THE SOLVABILITY GATE, not by any prior check. targetX=4 makes highFeedback DEAD -- surveyed every OTHER derivativeTrace point-mode usage in the corpus and every single one sits in [-3,3]; 4 is the sole outlier and the sole failure. derivativeTrace's schema declares no explicit x-range (targetX and start are both plain z.number() with no min/max), so this is frontend-component behaviour invisible to schema.ts -- the same shape as triangleSolve's missing angleStep (S203T). Reverted to the sealed pre-session bytes; f(x)=x squared restricted to x>=0 genuinely needs x=4 (f-inverse of 16), and no smaller target represents the same fact. Refused.
